Content:
Any set of two vectors that contains the zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{0}] must be linearly dependent. To see this, consider the set [MATH: \left\{ \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{0} \right\}.] We can realize that this set is linearly dependent using either of the following two methods.

Content:
Method 1

Content:
Notice that
[MATH: 0 \cdot \mathbf{v} + 1 \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Therefore, the equation
[MATH: x_1 \mathbf{v} + x_2 \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}]
has a solution [MATH: x_1=0] and [MATH: x_2=1,] which is different from [MATH: x_1=x_2=0.] So, the set is linearly dependent.

Content:
Method 2

Content:
Alternatively, recall that a set of two vectors is linearly dependent if and only if the two vectors are parallel. That is, the two vectors are multiples of each other.

Content:
The zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{0}] is parallel to every other vector because it is a multiple of any other vector. For any vector [MATH: \mathbf{v},] we have
[MATH: \mathbf{0} = 0 \cdot \mathbf{v} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \mathbf{0} \parallel \mathbf{v}.]

Content:
So, because [MATH: \mathbf{0}] is parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{v},] the set [MATH: \left\{ \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{0} \right\}] is linearly dependent.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We say that two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] are linearly independent if the only solution to the equation
[MATH: x_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{0}]
is [MATH: x_1 = x_2 = 0.] Otherwise, if there exists any solution other than [MATH: x_1 = x_2 = 0,] then we say that the two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] are linearly dependent.

Content:
To illustrate, let's consider two sets of vectors in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [1; 0]]

Content:
- For the first set [MATH: {\color{blue}(\textrm{I})},] we have
[MATH: x_{1}a_{1} + x_{2}a_{2}|= 0; x_{1}[1; 0] + x_{2}[0; 1]|= 0.]
The above equation is true only if [MATH: x_1=x_2=0.] So, the set [MATH: \color{blue}(\textrm{I})] is linearly independent.
- On the other hand, for the second set [MATH: {\color{red}(\textrm{II})},] we have
[MATH: x_{1}b_{1} + x_{2}b_{2}|= 0; x_{1}[1; 1] + x_{2}[− 2; − 2]|= 0.]
The above equation has solutions other than [MATH: x_1=x_2=0.] For example, [MATH: x_1=2] and [MATH: x_2=1] gives
[MATH: [1; 1]]
Therefore, the set [MATH: \color{red}(\textrm{II})] is not linearly independent. Rather, it is linearly dependent.

Content:
Note: You may notice that the vectors in the set [MATH: \color{red}(\textrm{II})] were parallel (i.e. multiples of one another), while the vectors in set [MATH: \color{blue}(\textrm{I})] were not. This trend holds in general, for all sets of two vectors:

Content:
- a set of two vectors is linearly dependent if and only if the two vectors are parallel, while
- a set of two vectors is linearly independent if and only if the two vectors are not parallel.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Sets of Two Vectors Containing the Zero Vector

Content:
Any set of two vectors that contains the zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{0}] must be linearly dependent. To see this, consider the set [MATH: \left\{ \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{0} \right\}.] We can realize that this set is linearly dependent using either of the following two methods.

Content:
Method 1

Content:
Notice that
[MATH: 0 \cdot \mathbf{v} + 1 \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Therefore, the equation
[MATH: x_1 \mathbf{v} + x_2 \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}]
has a solution [MATH: x_1=0] and [MATH: x_2=1,] which is different from [MATH: x_1=x_2=0.] So, the set is linearly dependent.

Content:
Method 2

Content:
Alternatively, recall that a set of two vectors is linearly dependent if and only if the two vectors are parallel. That is, the two vectors are multiples of each other.

Content:
The zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{0}] is parallel to every other vector because it is a multiple of any other vector. For any vector [MATH: \mathbf{v},] we have
